title: Systemic pharmacological access to brain parenchyma for arbitrary drug classes

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a broadly reusable way to administer drugs systemically and obtain predictable, therapeutically useful exposure in human brain parenchyma—the functional tissue of the brain. Its intended scope includes efflux-substrate small molecules, proteins, and oligonucleotides, together with measurement and control of exposure in peripheral tissues and brain blood vessels. Success would mean that active drug reaches its intended tissue and cellular targets at tolerable doses. Drug detected in blood supplying the brain, or a change in cerebrospinal fluid alone, would not establish this capability. This is the proposed scope, rather than an achieved general delivery system.

Existing engineered delivery approaches provide a technical basis for the idea. A transferrin-receptor transport vehicle has delivered antisense oligonucleotides into animal CNS tissue, while an enzyme fused to an anti-transferrin-receptor antibody has been studied intravenously in people with Hunter syndrome. These examples show how receptor-mediated transport can help particular engineered cargos overcome delivery limitations. They do not establish a general rule that the same system will transport arbitrary drugs with predictable distribution.

significance.text: A drug intended to act directly on a target in brain parenchyma needs sufficient active exposure at that target. The supplied evidence illustrates this constraint for antisense oligonucleotides and the unmodified enzyme iduronate-2-sulfatase: poor delivery limits the usefulness of systemic administration for CNS action. Engineered transport can connect systemic dosing to brain pharmacology, as illustrated by animal RNA knockdown and the PMDA report's account of reduced brain heparan sulfate in mice receiving pabinafusp alfa.

Conditional significance: a delivery capability that generalized across modalities would remove a major constraint on CNS drug design. Researchers could consider a wider range of therapeutic molecules without having to solve systemic brain entry separately for every cargo. The immediate advance would be improved distribution and target access. Better treatments would remain conditional on choosing useful disease targets, delivering active drug to the relevant cells and intracellular compartments, and achieving effective pharmacology without unacceptable toxicity. A drug can also influence the CNS indirectly without entering brain tissue, so the exposure requirement applies specifically to direct parenchymal action.

Brain access would not by itself establish selective brain delivery. The 2024 oligonucleotide transport study also reported functional RNA knockdown in mouse quadriceps and cardiac muscle. That finding makes peripheral pharmacology a concrete consideration; it does not itself demonstrate peripheral toxicity. The revolutionary outcome would require a usable therapeutic index across the relevant tissues. Indiscriminate barrier opening that produces unacceptable brain toxicity would fail that goal.

Scope distinction: this concept overlaps substantially with a universal macromolecular blood–brain barrier shuttle, but extends beyond it by explicitly including efflux-substrate small molecules and constraints on exposure away from the intended target. Even a highly effective macromolecular shuttle would therefore address only part of the proposed capability. No numerical claim about the fraction of drugs excluded by the barrier is needed to establish the significance.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability proposed here is reliable generalization: predictable human parenchymal exposure across substantially different cargos, rather than successful transport of a specially engineered molecule. The supplied sources document that antisense oligonucleotides do not readily cross the mammalian blood–brain barrier and that unmodified iduronate-2-sulfatase has a specific CNS delivery limitation. They also document engineered approaches to those limitations. They do not establish the full physical and transporter-selectivity account for every modality in this concept, or determine whether the broader capability remains unavailable as of 1 November 2026.

Engineering synthesis: a general platform would need to move active cargo beyond the vascular compartment, distribute it through relevant brain regions, and deliver it to the cells and subcellular sites where it must act. It would also need predictable dose–exposure relationships despite changes in cargo properties. For the proposed small-molecule scope, entry would have to yield adequate exposure despite relevant efflux processes. For proteins and oligonucleotides, transport would have to preserve activity and enable access to the appropriate cellular destination. The supplied evidence does not show that one architecture can satisfy all of these requirements.

Translation and safety remain separate barriers to broad applicability. The animal oligonucleotide results do not establish therapeutic human delivery, and their peripheral activity does not establish sparing of tissues where a particular drug should not act. The human enzyme-fusion evidence concerns a single product in one disease; the PMDA review also called for further evaluation of long-term efficacy and safety. A reusable platform would need to resolve these questions for different cargos and disease settings rather than inherit assurances from either example.

current_state.text: Barker and colleagues' study, published on 14 August 2024, reported a transferrin-receptor-targeting oligonucleotide transport vehicle. According to the supplied abstract, systemic administration produced sustained Malat1 RNA knockdown across multiple CNS regions and cell types in mice engineered to express human transferrin receptor. In cynomolgus macaques, a vehicle targeting MALAT1 produced more uniform CNS biodistribution and target-RNA knockdown than intrathecal administration of the same unconjugated antisense oligonucleotide. The authors characterized the approach as a potential platform for therapeutic ASO delivery. These are animal delivery and tool-RNA results, not demonstrations of therapeutic efficacy in humans or compatibility across drug classes.

The same abstract states that antisense oligonucleotides do not readily cross the mammalian blood–brain barrier and therefore require intrathecal delivery for CNS use in the context described. It also reports systemic-vehicle-mediated Malat1 knockdown in mouse quadriceps and cardiac muscles. Thus, the study supports functional delivery within and beyond the CNS, rather than selective brain exposure. The supplied review assessed the abstract, not the full paper; detailed methods, quantitative effect sizes, and the full safety evidence cannot be reconstructed from this record.

Okuyama and colleagues' phase 2/3 study, published in February 2021, administered intravenous pabinafusp alfa—iduronate-2-sulfatase fused to an anti-human-transferrin-receptor antibody—to 28 Japanese patients with Hunter syndrome, also called mucopolysaccharidosis type II, for 52 weeks. The trial was multicenter, single-arm, and open-label. Cerebrospinal-fluid heparan sulfate concentrations decreased from baseline to week 52, with a reported p value below 0.001. This is disease-specific human evidence relevant to CNS delivery and pharmacological activity. CSF substrate reduction does not directly quantify predictable exposure throughout human brain parenchyma, and the uncontrolled trial design limits causal interpretation of broader clinical outcomes.

The clinical study was available to the supplied review through an abstract record and captions, without inspected figure data or full methods. Consequently, the retained evidence supports the trial design, treatment duration, patient count, and reported CSF biomarker result, but does not support an independent assessment of the full data or a stronger claim of generalized parenchymal delivery.

The 2021 PMDA report for Izcargo concluded that pabinafusp alfa had efficacy in mucopolysaccharidosis type II and could be approved subject to conditions, including further evaluation of long-term efficacy and safety. The efficacy conclusion appears under Results of Review. The supplied extraction ends during page 38 and is truncated. It supports the attributed regulatory assessment, but does not verify the separately reported sponsor announcement or final approval event dated 23 March 2021. That approval claim remains unverified within the supplied record; this limitation is not evidence that approval did not occur.

Evidence boundary: these dated studies establish particular engineered delivery achievements, not arbitrary-cargo access. The supplied search record contains no freshness assessment sufficient to establish the complete state of the field on 1 November 2026. The record therefore supports neither a claim that this general capability has been achieved nor a definitive claim that it remains absent on that date.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed initial demonstration: after systemic dosing in humans, one platform should achieve therapeutically relevant target engagement in brain parenchyma using representative efflux-substrate small molecules, proteins, and oligonucleotides, across more than one disease. Peripheral and vascular exposure should be measured and compatible with a usable therapeutic index. Three modality classes and multiple diseases are proposed milestones for demonstrating breadth, not established regulatory or scientific standards.
completion_criteria.label: Human therapeutic parenchymal engagement across three modalities and multiple diseases

completion_criteria.text: Proposed evidence requirements: studies should distinguish active drug and target engagement in parenchyma from drug retained in brain blood vessels or inferred delivery from CSF biomarkers alone. They should characterize dose, exposure, duration of action, regional and cellular coverage, and relevant adverse effects. Direct tissue measurements or validated compartment-sensitive methods would need to justify the inference of parenchymal action, with uncertainty stated where human sampling is limited.
completion_criteria.label: Compartment-sensitive evidence distinguishes active parenchymal drug action from vascular retention

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: results should be reproducible in independent studies and across representative cargos, with explicit reporting of failed cargos, disease contexts, dosing limits, and repeat-dose tolerability. Operational thresholds for therapeutic target engagement and acceptable exposure should be specified for each cargo and indication before evaluating success. A finite test program could demonstrate breadth and define a useful operating range; it could not prove literal applicability to arbitrary drugs.
completion_criteria.label: Independent reproducibility across cargos with prespecified thresholds and reported limits

completion_criteria.text: The existing animal tool-RNA knockdown and human enzyme-associated CSF substrate reduction would be useful components of such a program. They address important parts of delivery and pharmacology, but neither alone satisfies the proposed human, cross-modality, compartment-sensitive demonstration.
completion_criteria.label: Animal knockdown and human CSF substrate reduction alone remain insufficient

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: PHA-11, reliable oral systemic exposure for folded peptides and proteins, addresses getting intact drugs into the systemic circulation. PHA-05 addresses their subsequent access to brain tissue after systemic dosing. The two capabilities could be combined, but solving oral absorption would not establish brain delivery. PHA-13, a medicine that holds its own therapeutic window without an external controller, concerns autonomous control of drug action or exposure. It could complement PHA-05's therapeutic-index requirement, but predictable brain access does not itself confer that control.

Roster-based synthesis: PHA-01, pharmacological control of proteins without usable binding pockets, concerns whether a drug can act on a target; PHA-05 concerns whether it can reach a brain target. PHA-07, dismantling pathogenic protein conformations and restoring function, could depend on PHA-05 for systemically administered CNS treatments, while retaining the separate challenge of reversing the pathogenic conformation. PHA-10, severe analgesia uncoupled from respiratory depression and reinforcement, concerns separation of therapeutic and adverse pharmacology. Better CNS distribution might assist a particular design, but would not by itself produce that separation.

Roster-based synthesis: PHA-02, prospective prediction of human efficacy, dose, and major toxicity, would require reliable models of brain and peripheral exposure for relevant drugs. Achieving delivery would not establish predictive accuracy before human exposure. PHA-03, prevention of idiosyncratic immune-mediated drug injury, addresses a distinct safety problem that successful delivery would not resolve. PHA-04, antigen-chosen control of immune memory, specifies selective immune intervention; PHA-05 supplies a potential delivery capability only where such an intervention requires direct brain access.

Roster-based synthesis: PHA-06, in-place replacement of missing human cell types, and PHA-12, scarless regrowth of complex adult mammalian structures, require biological reconstruction beyond transport. Brain access could enable delivery of relevant effectors in CNS applications without demonstrating cell replacement or regrowth. PHA-09, changing the human aging rate across organ systems, has a broader organism-level endpoint; CNS delivery could be one enabling component but would not establish altered aging. PHA-08, eradication of dormant infectious persisters without seeding genetic resistance, concerns antimicrobial action and resistance; PHA-05 becomes relevant when the infectious reservoir requiring treatment is in brain tissue.

unresolved_issues: The complete state of systemic brain-delivery platforms as of 1 November 2026 is unassessed because no freshness search entries were supplied.
The final Japanese approval event and reported 23 March 2021 sponsor announcement require a retained supporting source.
The supplied evidence does not establish delivery performance for efflux-substrate small molecules or a comprehensive physical and transporter-selectivity account across the proposed modalities.
The ASO evidence was reviewed at abstract level; the clinical trial record included abstract text and captions without inspected figure data or full methods, and the PMDA extraction was truncated.
Human parenchymal exposure, cross-cargo generalization, peripheral sparing, and long-term tolerability remain unresolved for the broad proposed platform.
The proposed demonstration still requires indication-specific definitions of therapeutic target engagement, acceptable peripheral and vascular exposure, reproducibility, and repeat-dose safety.

brief.title: Reliable delivery of many kinds of drugs into the brain
possible: Patients could receive drugs through the bloodstream that reliably reach the brain tissue where they need to act. A reusable delivery system would work with proteins, oligonucleotides—short strands of genetic material—and small drugs that the brain normally pumps out.
why: Researchers could choose from a wider range of molecules for treating brain diseases without solving brain entry separately for every drug. Predictable delivery would help them get enough active drug to the cells where it is needed.

sources.who: Scarlett J Barker and colleagues at Denali Therapeutics and Ionis Pharmaceuticals
sources.showed: Their carrier delivered oligonucleotides from the bloodstream into mouse and monkey brain tissue and reduced targeted genetic molecules. It also acted in mouse skeletal and heart muscle.
sources.quote:
In addition, systemic delivery of OTV enabled
Malat1
RNA knockdown in mouse quadriceps and cardiac muscles, which are difficult to target with oligonucleotides alone.
sources.cited_for: Engineered carriers can deliver active genetic drugs into animal brain tissue, while also producing effects elsewhere.
sources.not_established: Animal results do not establish therapeutic delivery in humans or reliable transport of different drug classes.

sources.showed: An uncontrolled trial in people with Hunter syndrome tested pabinafusp alfa, an enzyme joined to a transport antibody. Treatment reduced accumulated material in the fluid around the brain.
sources.quote: HS concentrations in the CSF significantly decreased from baseline to week 52
sources.cited_for: A specially engineered enzyme given through the bloodstream produced a disease-related change in fluid around the human brain.
sources.not_established: A fluid measurement does not establish active drug throughout brain tissue, and the trial lacked a comparison group.

sources.showed: Japan's drug regulator concluded that pabinafusp alfa was effective for Hunter syndrome and had acceptable safety relative to its benefits. It called for further evaluation of long-term effects.
sources.quote:
On the basis of the data submitted, PMDA has concluded that the product has efficacy in the treatment of  
mucopolysaccharidosis type II , and that the product has acceptable  safety in view of its benefits  (see 
Attachment).
sources.cited_for: A regulator judged a particular engineered enzyme effective for a particular disease.
sources.not_established: That assessment does not establish a reusable delivery system or long-term safety across different drugs.

shown: Barker and colleagues delivered genetic drugs into animal brains. In monkeys, delivery through the bloodstream spread the drug more evenly and reduced its genetic target more than injection into spinal fluid.

Okuyama and colleagues tested an engineered enzyme in 28 people with Hunter syndrome. It reduced accumulated material in fluid around the brain, but that does not directly measure delivery into working brain tissue.
missing: A shared system has yet to demonstrate useful human brain delivery across the proposed drug classes and diseases.
Active drug must reach the right brain regions, cells and locations inside cells at predictable doses.
Repeated treatment must remain tolerable while controlling exposure in brain blood vessels and the rest of the body.

milestones.label: Human brain action across drug classes and diseases
milestones.explanation: One system would have to produce therapeutic brain action with small drugs normally pumped out, proteins and oligonucleotides across multiple diseases, with tolerable exposure elsewhere. This would demonstrate breadth.

milestones.label: Active drug action distinguished from blood-vessel retention
milestones.explanation: Measurements would have to distinguish active drug in brain tissue from drug in blood vessels, tracking dose, duration, coverage and harms. This would establish where the drug acts beyond changes in surrounding fluid.

milestones.label: Independent studies reproduce results and define limits
milestones.explanation: Independent studies would have to repeat results across drugs using preset success thresholds and report failures, dosing limits and repeated-dose tolerability. This would define a useful operating range.

milestones.label: Animal and brain-fluid findings remain insufficient alone
milestones.explanation: Animal genetic-target reductions and human brain-fluid changes would have to contribute to a broader human demonstration. Neither result alone establishes active brain delivery across drug classes.

uncertain: Can a shared delivery system work across drugs with very different properties, including small molecules the brain pumps out?
What counts as enough drug action and acceptable exposure elsewhere will depend on the drug and disease.
Limited access to human brain tissue complicates judging whether measurements truly establish action in the intended cells.

page.title: Systemic drug delivery to brain parenchyma
page.definition: A reusable platform would carry drugs from the bloodstream into human brain parenchyma, the tissue containing neurons and glia beyond the blood vessel wall. With the same transport mechanism, a protein, an oligonucleotide (a short strand of DNA or RNA) and a small molecule whose entry is normally limited by efflux pumps would each act on its target in that tissue. The response would vary with dose within each drug’s safety limits.

goal.need: About two-thirds of people with Hunter syndrome develop progressive cognitive impairment. Conventional intravenous idursulfase treats physical symptoms, but the blood–brain barrier limits how much enzyme reaches the brain. A reusable carrier could let patients with metabolic or neurodegenerative disease receive a wider range of drugs by infusion and avoid repeated procedures to deliver them into cerebrospinal fluid. Whether a given drug slows cognitive decline still requires clinical evidence.

figures.caption: Cerebrospinal-fluid heparan sulfate during intravenous pabinafusp alfa treatment for Hunter syndrome.
figures.note: Uncontrolled study: 28 patients received 2 mg/kg weekly. Missing week-52 values were imputed from the closest available measurement. Cerebrospinal fluid surrounds the brain and spinal cord; its substrate concentration does not directly measure drug exposure in brain tissue.

completion.title: One platform demonstrates systemic human brain delivery across all three cargo classes.
completion.criterion: One delivery platform, retaining its transport mechanism across cargos, delivers at least one efflux-substrate small molecule, protein and oligonucleotide systemically in people. Each meets prespecified brain target-engagement and safety endpoints with a measured dose–exposure–response relationship. Compartment-sensitive evidence establishes active drug action in brain parenchyma beyond vascular retention or cerebrospinal-fluid changes alone. Independent investigators reproduce the human findings. The result establishes the tested cargo range.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; no outside body located defines completion for this combined cargo scope.
completion.basis: Searches of IMI2 BBB calls, NIH TARGETED prize documents, FDA/PMDA product documents, standards and developer platform filings found no cross-class human completion criterion. This bounded test combines the stated cargo scope, NIMH's tolerated-dose target-engagement gate and IMI2's call for independent validation. A finite demonstration establishes applicability to tested cargos.

milestones.title: A delivery target increases animal brain exposure to an antibody or ligand that binds it.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate increased in vivo brain exposure to an antibody or ligand of the proposed delivery target. IMI2 specifies no minimum fold increase.
milestones.set_by: IMI2 Joint Undertaking, 12th Call, Topic 6, work package 5. The published validation criterion names antibodies and ligands.
milestones.threshold_quote: Validated new brain-delivery targets (by demonstration of increased in vivo brain exposure of Ab or ligand of the target).

milestones.title: A brain-delivery cargo produces a significant, dose-related pharmacological response in nonclinical studies.
milestones.criterion: Establish the cargo's dose/concentration–response relationship, significant pharmacological effects and active form in nonclinical studies; assess major physiological functions before human dosing. Barker and colleagues reported systemic antisense-oligonucleotide delivery with target-RNA reduction in mice and cynomolgus macaques. The accessible abstract does not establish the complete dose–response and safety package.
milestones.set_by: Japan's Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare, Guidance for Establishing Safety in First-in-Human Studies during Drug Development, sections 3.3.2–3.3.4. This is general drug-development guidance.
milestones.threshold_quote: sufficient dose levels to detect significant pharmacological effects and to identify the active form of the drug.

milestones.title: An authorised clinical study administers a systemic brain-delivery drug to people.
milestones.criterion: Administer the investigational drug systemically to a participant after the required regulatory and ethics authorisations. For a US study requiring an investigational new drug application, the review board must approve the study and the application must be in effect. It takes effect 30 days after FDA receives it unless FDA imposes a clinical hold, or earlier if FDA notifies the sponsor that the investigation may begin.
milestones.set_by: FDA, 21 CFR 312.21(a)(1), 312.40 and 312.66, covering first human investigation, an effective investigational new drug application and institutional review board approval.
milestones.threshold_quote: Phase 1 includes the initial introduction of an investigational new drug into humans.

milestones.title: A systemic cargo engages its CNS target dose-dependently at a tolerated dose in people.
milestones.criterion: After systemic administration in people, demonstrate a dose-dependent effect at the proposed site of drug action in the central nervous system. Meet the study’s prespecified quantitative threshold for functional target engagement and provide preliminary evidence of tolerability at the same dose range. NIMH leaves the numerical target-engagement threshold to the study.
milestones.set_by: NIMH, PAR-25-184, R61-to-R33 go/no-go criteria. The criterion was published for mental-disorder interventions, rather than delivery platforms or particular cargo classes.
milestones.threshold_quote: demonstrate that the intervention displays dose/stimulation-dependent effects at the proposed site of action

milestones.title: A delivery candidate shows transport across a validated blood–brain barrier model.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate passage of the candidate across an in vitro blood–brain barrier model validated with reference compounds whose transport across the barrier is known in vivo. The programme specifies no minimum permeability or fold increase for a candidate.
milestones.set_by: Innovative Medicines Initiative 2 Joint Undertaking, 12th Call, Topic 6, work package 3.
milestones.threshold_quote: validate model with a set of reference compounds with known in vivo BBB transport data, validate candidates in vitro

milestones.title: Nonclinical studies establish the cargo’s dose–response relationship and identify its active form.
milestones.criterion: Test enough dose or concentration levels to establish how the pharmacological response varies, identify the principal pharmacological effect and identify the active form of the drug.
milestones.set_by: Japan’s Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare, revised first-in-human guidance, section 3.3.2.
milestones.threshold_quote: 薬理学的作用の用量(濃度)相関性は，主要な薬理作用及び活性本体を特定するために，十分な用量段階を用いて検討すべきである．

milestones.title: Nonclinical studies characterize the drug’s effects on vital functions before human dosing.
milestones.criterion: Characterize functional effects on the cardiovascular, respiratory and central nervous systems before first human administration. Assess other organ systems when warranted by the drug.
milestones.set_by: Japan’s Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare, revised first-in-human guidance, section 3.3.4.
milestones.threshold_quote: ヒト初回投与前には，主要な生理的機能(例えば，心血管系，中枢神経系及び呼吸器系)に及ぼす機能的な影響を明らかにすべきである

not_found: No published completion criterion was found for one systemic human brain-delivery platform covering all three cargo classes.
No human study was found demonstrating the complete cross-class capability defined here.
No regulator, society or programme statement was found opposing pursuit of systemic brain delivery across the three cargo classes.

results.finding: Systemic OTV delivery produced target-RNA knockdown in macaque CNS; sample size and numerical effect were not reported.
results.detail: The abstract does not establish a dose–response relationship, statistical significance, or assessment of major physiological functions.
results.quote:

definition = "A reusable platform would carry drugs from the bloodstream into human brain parenchyma, the tissue containing neurons and glia beyond the blood vessel wall. With the same transport mechanism, a protein, an oligonucleotide (a short strand of DNA or RNA) and a small molecule whose entry is normally limited by efflux pumps would each act on its target in that tissue. The response would vary with dose within each drug\u2019s safety limits.". Reason: The definition now locates drug action beyond the vessel wall and explains how efflux can restrict entry into the brain.

goal.need = "About two-thirds of people with Hunter syndrome develop progressive cognitive impairment. Conventional intravenous idursulfase treats physical symptoms, but the blood\u2013brain barrier limits how much enzyme reaches the brain. A reusable carrier could let patients with metabolic or neurodegenerative disease receive a wider range of drugs by infusion and avoid repeated procedures to deliver them into cerebrospinal fluid. Whether a given drug slows cognitive decline still requires clinical evidence.". Reason: The proportion of patients at risk of cognitive decline describes the unmet need more directly than prior treatment in one trial cohort.

add milestone after None: "A delivery candidate shows transport across a validated blood–brain barrier model.". Reason: IMI2 specifies an in vitro test of transport candidates before its separate animal brain-exposure test.

edit m1: title = "A delivery target increases animal brain exposure to an antibody or ligand that binds it."; criterion = "Demonstrate increased in vivo brain exposure to an antibody or ligand of the proposed delivery target. IMI2 specifies no minimum fold increase."; threshold_quote = "Validated new brain-delivery targets (by demonstration of increased in vivo brain exposure of Ab or ligand of the target)."; threshold_ref = 7; refs = [7]. Reason: IMI2 specifies exposure to the target’s antibody or ligand, and the fold increase observed for ANG1005 is a study result.

split m2 into "Nonclinical studies establish the cargo’s dose–response relationship and identify its active form." | "Nonclinical studies characterize the drug’s effects on vital functions before human dosing.". Reason: Japan’s guidance defines drug activity and effects on vital functions in separate sections, so a study that establishes one can be judged on that result.
